subject: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course

messages.author: ecf19e9eac4d03c4
messages.subject: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
parts:
Dear Stan users group,

We are interested in implementing in Stan (through RStan) a Gaussian
Process negative binomial regression model for (RNA-seq) gene expression
time-courses. The original publication's model is implemented in Matlab
and it runs quite slowly, i.e. it takes > 30 mins per gene and we have
~40K genes in our dataset. So, we would like to implement this model in
Stan in order to speed it up, and also to improve on the manner in which
differential gene expression is assessed (see below). We would greatly
appreciate the Stan community's help in implementing this model; the
original publication with the model is attached.

As mentioned, an additional concern is how to determine if a gene is
differentially expressed. The original publication used Bayes Factors
between a model in which two conditions or tissues are modeled
separately (H1) and one in which they're modeled together (H0). From
what I've read on the Stan users group, you would probably recommend
using WAIC to compare models, correct?

The original paper used the harmonic mean estimator of the marginal
likelihood, which I know is a terrible estimator. Nevertheless, I
noticed that Stan doesn't implement any path sampling method for
marginal likelihood estimation, so Bayes Factors are not a possibility
in Stan.

For background purposes, we have a well replicated time-course of two
tissues that were sampled every 2 hours for 2 days. The above model is
run on a gene-by-gene basis and then it's determined whether H1 or H0
better fits the data in order to assess differential gene expression.

Any guidance/help would be much appreciated! ...I've been following the
development of Stan, but haven't yet had time or the need (until now) to
learn how to use it.

Thanks!
Dan Fulop.
--
Daniel Fulop, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Scholar
Dept. Plant Biology, UC Davis
Maloof Lab, Rm. 2220
Life Sciences Addition, One Shields Ave.
Davis, CA 95616

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
parts:
I had a quick look through the paper. I think you should be able to get much faster inference with Stan and maybe even something useful for 40K genes. For even faster inference I would suggest using distributional approximations (Laplace, VB, EP). For example, GPstuff toolbox could be used for negative Binomial GP, although it doesn't yet have time varying time scaling.

I recommend LOO-CV with truncated importance sampling instead of WAIC, as it as easy to compute and has a smaller bias in case of surprising observations.
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf

Aki

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
parts:
The GP model can be simplified substantially by thinking of the
GP are more of a generalized linear model instead of trying to
parameterize the mean and variance.  For example,

Sigma1 <- Covariance matrix for first GP
Sigma 2 <- Covariance matrix for second GP

f1 ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma1);
f2 ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma2);

for (n in 1:n_data)
 y[n] ~ negative_binomial( exp(f1[n]), exp(f2[n]) );

(careful about the parameterizations — this is the overdispersion
parameterization nominally used in in Stan, not the p, r 
parameterization).

This kind of data is begging to be fit hierarchically over the genes
(and patients, if measurements were made across a population)
— it would be hard to fit over 40,000 genes but you would get much
better inferences.  In the end you have to figure out wether a simple
but probably biased model that fits over all 40,000 genes is better
or worse than a complex model that fits over few genes but can
incorporate more complexities that arise in the data.  Not something
we can determine a priori, but something you can explore with Stan!

Lastly, if you’re trying to compare modelings using predictive
performance (cross validation, information criteria, etc) then
you have to recognize that you’ve lost the Occam effect in
the marginal likelihood and you won’t have any preference
for the simpler zero-differential model.  One of the immediate
consequences of this is that you can just fit a model with
differential responses and rephrase your question in terms
of an expectation like what is the probability of

P[ | response1 -  response2 | > epsilon ]

for some epsilon (or perhaps a bunch of epsilons).

Hi Michael,

Thanks for your detailed response.

On Monday, April 13, 2015 at 3:09:17 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
The GP model can be simplified substantially by thinking of the
GP are more of a generalized linear model instead of trying to
parameterize the mean and variance.  For example,

f2 ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma2);

for (n in 1:n_data)

I get the idea of using a finite number of multivariate normals instead of a full Gaussian Process.  We would have to play around with the data to see how many multi_normals we would need.  Thanks for the suggestion!

(careful about the parameterizations — this is the overdispersion
parameterization nominally used in in Stan, not the p, r 
parameterization).

This kind of data is begging to be fit hierarchically over the genes
(and patients, if measurements were made across a population)

I know!  I toyed with the idea of asking that in my initial email and decided to leave it out for simplicity's sake and because it's perhaps a bit of a "can of worms."

All genomic scale datasets beg for a joint hierarchical model, but the problem with such models is the heterogeneity in genome scale data.  For instance, some genes have sine-shaped expression time-courses (not necessarily with coinciding peaks and troughs), whereas others have a single peak at a given time of day, and yet others may be roughly invariant throughout the day  ...and others may monotonically decrease or increase through the time-course

Forgive me if I'm wrong, but I think this sort of heterogeneity would require gene clustering as part of the model fitting  ...say with a Dirichlet Process prior or the Gaussian Process approximations of the DPP that I've read about in the Stan list.  One intermediate 2-stage alternative would be to first cluster the genes without "looking" at their expression patterns and then to use a relatively simple hierarchical negative binomial GP to model clusters of covarying genes. This would be practical, though not very Bayesian minded.

...for what it's worth, it's plants and not patients we're dealing with.

— it would be hard to fit over 40,000 genes but you would get much
better inferences.  In the end you have to figure out wether a simple
but probably biased model that fits over all 40,000 genes is better

Given the sort of heterogeneities in time-courses that we know exist in the data, I'd lean towards a somewhat complex hierarchical model or a gene-by-gene approach. What sorts of hierarchical models would you suggest could accommodate this heterogeneity?

Not something
we can determine a priori, but something you can explore with Stan!
I'm happy to explore, but we already know there's a lot of heterogeneity in time-courses.

performance (cross validation, information criteria, etc) then

Thanks for suggesting this!  I rather like this idea.  I'll ask for feedback about reasonable epsilon values when the time comes.

parts: I get the idea of using a finite number of multivariate normals instead of a full Gaussian Process.  We would have to play around with the data to see how many multi_normals we would need.  Thanks for the suggestion!

Oh, I was just suggesting the more direct

mu[n] = exp(f1[n])

instead of the 

mu[n] = exp(f1[n]) / ( exp(f1[n]) + sigma[n] )

used in the paper (or whatever the right equation is — I’m going off the top of my head).

The multivariate normal is how you implement _any_ GP in practice,
it’s just particularly transparent in Stan.

I know!  I toyed with the idea of asking that in my initial email and decided to leave it out for simplicity's sake and because it's perhaps a bit of a "can of worms."

All genomic scale datasets beg for a joint hierarchical model, but the problem with such models is the heterogeneity in genome scale data.  For instance, some genes have sine-shaped expression time-courses (not necessarily with coinciding peaks and troughs), whereas others have a single peak at a given time of day, and yet others may be roughly invariant throughout the day  ...and others may monotonically decrease or increase through the time-course

Forgive me if I'm wrong, but I think this sort of heterogeneity would require gene clustering as part of the model fitting  ...say with a Dirichlet Process prior or the Gaussian Process approximations of the DPP that I've read about in the Stan list.  One intermediate 2-stage alternative would be to first cluster the genes without "looking" at their expression patterns and then to use a relatively simple hierarchical negative binomial GP to model clusters of covarying genes. This would be practical, though not very Bayesian minded.

...for what it's worth, it's plants and not patients we're dealing with.

Given the sort of heterogeneities in time-courses that we know exist in the data, I'd lean towards a somewhat complex hierarchical model or a gene-by-gene approach. What sorts of hierarchical models would you suggest could accommodate this heterogeneity?

There’s a lot that can be done before resorting to Dirichlet processes!
One of the approaches we strongly recommend is to start simple and
add structure in stages.

So start with a small number of genes and fit everything independently
to gauge your computational budget.  Then you can consider very
simple hierarchical models, for example, making the length scale of
the GP hyperparameters hierarchical across each individual gene.
Adding more layers to the hierarchy, to take into account the varying
time-responses you note, can be considered much later on.

Personally I would put a little more thought into the measurement
model — if the measurement of gene expression is correlated then
any model that tries to measure differential expression while ignoring
the correlation will yield misleading results!  This is especially
important if any of that heterogeneity comes from environmental
factors that can be incorporated into the measurement model.
Thanks for suggesting this!  I rather like this idea.  I'll ask for feedback about reasonable epsilon values when the time comes.

There won’t be any particular value of epsilon — you’ll have to explore
the model and come up with some bespoke narrative appropriate to
the journal/funding agency/community.  For example, consider plotting 
the probability as a function of epsilon using the shape of the function
to construct a narrative.

Okay, pardon my ignorance. Certainly the NB dispersion is typically modeled hierarchically in RNAseq differential expression methods, although almost always in an empirical bayes fashion.  So, that could be modeled hierarchically for all genes; the assumption typically is that genes whose mean expression levels are similar have similar dispersion, so it's a mean-variance relationship that's modeled.

The function ShrinkSeq() (which is part of the ShrinkBayes) package implements a variety of RNAseq models that are more complex than that of other RNAseq software. ShrinkSeq isn't meant for time courses, but we could borrow some ideas from it. They hierarchically model several additional aspects apart from the dispersion, such as incorporating random effects (i.e. NB-GLMM) for experimental design variables (I suppose this sort of thing is what you are alluding to with regards to measurement error).

As to measurement error, I just spoke to Hagop (who actually did the tissue sampling and lab work) and the sampling was "pseudo-random" spatially (i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement), but no spatial information was recorded.  So, such information cannot be used to inform the model.  However, the plant field was relatively small (just 2 rows), etc.

One measurement error aspect that could be taken into account , though, is the sampling day.  Hagop has 3 replicates per time point per tissue, and 2 whole days of samples; all 3 replicates were sampled (i.e. frozen in liquid nitrogen) within ~10 minutes of each other .  So, we are planning to "collapse" both days to increase the time point replication to 6.  Conceivably sampling day could be assumed to influence the time-varying component of the model (not the heterogeneity of the time-course pattern, but rather the relative developmental acceleration/deceleration  ...i.e. the differential timing of cell maturation in the original paper); at least it's worth experimenting with such a specification.

So start with a small number of genes and fit everything independently
to gauge your computational budget.  Then you can consider very
simple hierarchical models, for example, making the length scale of
the GP hyperparameters hierarchical across each individual gene

What do you mean by the length scale?  What I'm gathering is that we would model the number of MVNs that make up the GP hierarchically so that there's a common distribution for all genes as to the number of MVNs, but then each gene would sample its MVN number from this common distribution.

.
Adding more layers to the hierarchy, to take into account the varying
time-responses you note, can be considered much later on.
That may not be necessary.  I think we can leave each gene to have its own time-varying response.  Otherwise we would need something like a DPP for that aspect of the model, I think.

Personally I would put a little more thought into the measurement
model — if the measurement of gene expression is correlated
What do you mean by correlated?  To what?

then
any model that tries to measure differential expression while ignoring
the correlation will yield misleading results!  This is especially
important if any of that heterogeneity comes from environmental
factors that can be incorporated into the measurement model.
As I said, the plant field was relatively small, and Hagop didn't keep track of the spatial sampling.  I would say that the environmental heterogeneity factors are relatively well controlled.

Thanks for suggesting this!  I rather like this idea.  I'll ask for feedback about reasonable epsilon values when the time comes.

There won’t be any particular value of epsilon — you’ll have to explore
the model and come up with some bespoke narrative appropriate to
the journal/funding agency/community.  For example, consider plotting 
the probability as a function of epsilon using the shape of the function
to construct a narrative.

Okay.  I had gotten then idea initially, but this further suggestion is quite informative.

We'll wait for Harri and Tarmo to post their Stan code and work from there to add hierarchical layers, etc.

Thanks,
Dan.

> On Apr 15, 2015, at 3:33 AM, Daniel Fulop <dfulo...@gmail.com> wrote:
...
> Okay, pardon my ignorance. Certainly the NB dispersion is typically modeled hierarchically in RNAseq differential expression methods, although almost always in an empirical bayes fashion.

Right --- there's Brad Efron's whole recent book. It's
what we'd call "maximum marginal likelihood" because Andrew
doesn't like "empirical Bayes" because of the connotation that
other Bayesian approaches aren't empirical.

Of course, we'd much rather do full Bayes and Stan's powerful enough to
do whole-genome modeling of this kind of differential expression
data.

> So, that could be modeled hierarchically for all genes; the assumption typically is that genes whose mean expression levels are similar have similar dispersion, so it's a mean-variance relationship that's modeled.

My understanding was that this didn't work very well and that there
was a huge amount of inter-experimental variation that wasn't accounted
for by a simple mean-variance relationship within or across experiments.

> The function ShrinkSeq() (which is part of the ShrinkBayes) package implements a variety of RNAseq models that are more complex than that of other RNAseq software. ShrinkSeq isn't meant for time courses, but we could borrow some ideas from it. So, such information cannot be used to inform the model. However, the plant field was relatively small (just 2 rows), etc.
>
> One measurement error aspect that could be taken into account , though, is the sampling day.

I'd also think you could take the basic sequencing data measurement into
account as well as the replication process that precedes it, which I believe
also has a huge amount of "lab hands" related variation, which is one of
the things that makes replication in this field so difficult.

> Hagop has 3 replicates per time point per tissue, and 2 whole days of samples; all 3 replicates were sampled (i.e. frozen in liquid nitrogen) within ~10 minutes of each other . So, we are planning to "collapse" both days to increase the time point replication to 6. Conceivably sampling day could be assumed to influence the time-varying component of the model (not the heterogeneity of the time-course pattern, but rather the relative developmental acceleration/deceleration ...i.e. the differential timing of cell maturation in the original paper); at least it's worth experimenting with such a specification.

I've seen some really neat work on circadian rhythm type analysis
out of Broad, where the same tissue is repeatedly sequenced over the
course of 24 hours or more (mainly with fruit flies in what I've seen).

>> So start with a small number of genes and fit everything independently
>> to gauge your computational budget. Then you can consider very
>> simple hierarchical models, for example, making the length scale of
>> the GP hyperparameters hierarchical across each individual gene
> What do you mean by the length scale? What I'm gathering is that we would model the number of MVNs that make up the GP hierarchically so that there's a common distribution for all genes as to the number of MVNs, but then each gene would sample its MVN number from this common distribution.

The length scale is a typical scale parameter --- it's in the
denominator of the squared exponential covariance matrix construction.
It controls how much the fitted function is allowed to wiggle --- that
is, how distance affects covariance.

>> .
>> Adding more layers to the hierarchy, to take into account the varying
>> time-responses you note, can be considered much later on.
> That may not be necessary. I think we can leave each gene to have its own time-varying response. Otherwise we would need something like a DPP for that aspect of the model, I think.

I don't think it'd need a DP, but then I'd also suggest starting
simple and seeing where the simple model doesn't fit using posterior
predictive checking.

>> Personally I would put a little more thought into the measurement
>> model — if the measurement of gene expression is correlated
> What do you mean by correlated? To what?

I'm guessing among the genes. At least that kind of co-expression is what
a lot of people are looking for to induce metabolic pathways. I
don't know how many genes your plants have, but we can't really scale
to a 40K x 40K correlation matrix! So what I've seen people do is try
to build something like "topic" models --- latent effects that account
for correlations in an implicitly low-rank sort of way.

And please keep us updated --- my wife used to work in this area and
I've been dying to do some work on gene expression measurement and
pathway induction. But I think I'll only have time to soak it up by proxy.

parts:
Okay, pardon my ignorance. Certainly the NB dispersion is typically modeled hierarchically in RNAseq differential expression methods, although almost always in an empirical bayes fashion.  So, that could be modeled hierarchically for all genes; the assumption typically is that genes whose mean expression levels are similar have similar dispersion, so it's a mean-variance relationship that's modeled.

The function ShrinkSeq() (which is part of the ShrinkBayes) package implements a variety of RNAseq models that are more complex than that of other RNAseq software. ShrinkSeq isn't meant for time courses, but we could borrow some ideas from it. They hierarchically model several additional aspects apart from the dispersion, such as incorporating random effects (i.e. NB-GLMM) for experimental design variables (I suppose this sort of thing is what you are alluding to with regards to measurement error).

As to measurement error, I just spoke to Hagop (who actually did the tissue sampling and lab work) and the sampling was "pseudo-random" spatially (i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement), but no spatial information was recorded.  So, such information cannot be used to inform the model.  However, the plant field was relatively small (just 2 rows), etc.

"i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement”
I understand the realities of the lab environment and appreciate
the candor, but statements like this make reproducibility supporters
cry a single tear at night.  ;-)

One measurement error aspect that could be taken into account , though, is the sampling day.  Hagop has 3 replicates per time point per tissue, and 2 whole days of samples; all 3 replicates were sampled (i.e. frozen in liquid nitrogen) within ~10 minutes of each other .  So, we are planning to "collapse" both days to increase the time point replication to 6.  Conceivably sampling day could be assumed to influence the time-varying component of the model (not the heterogeneity of the time-course pattern, but rather the relative developmental acceleration/deceleration  ...i.e. the differential timing of cell maturation in the original paper); at least it's worth experimenting with such a specification.

Yeah, a huge benefit of hierarchical modeling is that you don’t have
to “collapse” your data to try to improve statistical power.  

By measurement process I literally meant the physical process
that takes gene expression to some discrete counts on a computer.
Things like PCR, for example, confound different gene expressions
when trying to deconvolve the individual components and induce 
nontrivial correlations in the measured data that is often ignored.  
Reducing the entire measurement to “genes express proteins,
proteins magically turn into NB responses” is hugely simplified —
it may be sufficient for a given analysis but you have to be
prepared to argue that.  

We have lots of practice in finding flaws in oversimplified models...

What do you mean by the length scale?  What I'm gathering is that we would model the number of MVNs that make up the GP hierarchically so that there's a common distribution for all genes as to the number of MVNs, but then each gene would sample its MVN number from this common distribution.

I’m referring to the hyperparameters of the GP.  If you have the
heterogeneity in time responses that you claim (some increase,
some oscillate, some are constant, etc) then building a hierarchical
GP with common hyperparameters will not give you a good fit!

Really want you want to do is group the different time responses
and fit each individual group with an appropriate GP, perhaps
with the hyper parameters of those groups in a global hierarchy
themselves.
That may not be necessary.  I think we can leave each gene to have its own time-varying response.  Otherwise we would need something like a DPP for that aspect of the model, I think.

Again, there are a million things to do before looking at DPPs.
Even crude clustering combined with static hierarchical modeling
on those clusters can be hugely powerful, but you’ll have to spend
time informing those clusters using prior knowledge from experiment
and theory.  Good inferences don’t come cheap.

Anyways, start simple (say a hierarchy over each gene individually,
whether the hierarchy is over GPs or GP hyper parameters) and
build from there, incorporating time or spatial effects or clustering
the genes, etc.  Of course we’re happy to help in that process,
and a side benefit of starting simple is that it makes it easier for
us to understand your scientific motivations without having the
necessary background.
